task_description: Help me email the front desk staff about a new patient check-in procedure using tablets instead of paper forms — the system might have connectivity issues in our older building.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes clinic communications that prioritize patient safety and workflow continuity. Every process change is communicated with both the ideal flow and the fallback when things break. Treats email as a non-secure channel at all times.

rubric.name: Patient Flow Impact First
rubric.description: Changes are explained through their impact on patient experience and flow before the operational rationale. How many extra minutes per appointment, which rooms are affected, what the patient sees differently.

dimensions.label: The first substantive paragraph describes how the change affects patient experience or flow
Includes specific time estimates for how the change affects appointment duration or wait times
The business or compliance reason for the change appears after the patient impact, not before

rubric.name: Fallback Procedures Included
rubric.description: Every new process includes an explicit fallback for when the primary method fails. Clinical settings can't pause when technology breaks — staff need to know what to do when the system is down.

dimensions.label: Includes a specific 'if X fails, do Y instead' instruction
The fallback is a concrete procedure, not 'contact IT' or 'notify your manager'
Names the specific failure scenario the fallback addresses (system down, connectivity loss, etc.)

rubric.name: No Patient Identifiers
rubric.description: Never references patients by name in any email, even internal ones. Uses case numbers, room references, or appointment times. Email is treated as a non-secure channel regardless of policy.

dimensions.label: Does not include any patient names, initials, or uniquely identifying information
Refers to patients by case number, room number, appointment time, or generic reference
Does not include specific diagnoses, treatments, or medical details that could identify a patient in context

rubric.name: Bounded Process Steps
rubric.description: Multi-step processes use numbered steps, capped at 5. If a process needs more than 5 steps to explain in email, it needs a training session — the email should announce the training, not attempt to replace it.

dimensions.label: Processes with more than two actions use numbered steps
No process in the email exceeds 5 numbered steps
If a process is too complex for 5 steps, the email schedules training instead of attempting full documentation

rubric_used.coaching_notes: James's non-negotiable: every new process has a fallback. In clinical settings, 'the system is down' is not an edge case, it's a Tuesday. Will reject any email that names a patient or introduces a process without explaining what to do when it breaks.

rounds.draft:
**Subject:** New Tablet Check-In Process — Starting Monday, March 10

---

Hi Team,

Starting Monday, we're moving patient check-in from paper forms to tablets at the front desk. Here's what to expect and how to handle it if the technology doesn't cooperate.

**What Patients Will Notice**

Patients will be handed a tablet at arrival instead of a clipboard. The check-in form is the same information they're used to — it just lives on a screen now. For most patients, this won't change their wait time. For patients who need extra help navigating the tablet (unfamiliar with touchscreens, vision concerns, etc.), plan for an additional 3–5 minutes. If you're seeing back-to-back appointments, flag this at the start of your shift so the schedule can absorb it.

**The New Check-In Steps**

1. Greet the patient and hand them a sanitized tablet from the charging station.
2. Select their appointment time from the dropdown to pre-load their form.
3. Direct them to a seat and let them know you're available if they need help.
4. When they return the tablet, confirm the form is marked complete before routing them to the clinical area.
5. Return the tablet to the charging station.

**If the System Is Down or the Tablet Won't Connect**

Our building's Wi-Fi can be inconsistent, so this is a real possibility. If a tablet fails to load or shows a connectivity error:

- Use the paper backup forms kept in the **lower drawer of each front desk station** — they were restocked last week.
- Complete check-in on paper as usual and flag the appointment time on the paper log so the information can be entered into the system later.
- Do not delay rooming a patient while waiting for a tablet to reconnect.

**Why We're Making This Change**

This transition reduces transcription errors and speeds up records updates on the clinical side. It also reduces paper handling at the front desk over time.

If you have questions before Monday, reach out to me directly. We'll check in as a group after the first week to work through anything that needs adjusting.

Thanks,
[Your Name]
[Title]
[Contact]

criteria.justification: The first substantive paragraph ('What Patients Will Notice') leads with patient experience — what patients see, and a specific 3–5 minute estimate for patients needing extra help. The operational rationale ('reduces transcription errors') is correctly deferred to the final section. The quantified time impact is present but only for a subset of patients; no estimate is given for the typical patient, which slightly weakens the dimension. All three dimensions are substantially met.

The fallback section explicitly names the failure scenario (Wi-Fi inconsistency, tablet connectivity error), provides a concrete actionable procedure (paper forms in the lower drawer of each front desk station, flag the appointment time on the paper log), and instructs staff not to delay rooming. All three dimensions are clearly and fully satisfied.

No patient names, initials, or identifying information appear anywhere in the email. Patients are referred to generically ('the patient,' 'patients who need extra help') or by appointment time ('flag the appointment time on the paper log'). No clinical details are included. All three dimensions are fully met.

The check-in process is presented as exactly 5 numbered steps, meeting the cap precisely. The fallback uses bullets rather than numbered steps, which is appropriate for a short list of parallel actions rather than a sequential process. No process exceeds 5 steps, and the email does not attempt to document anything complex enough to require a training session. All three dimensions are satisfied.
